MEDI2200 · Week 10 · Lecture module — Cellular transport and trafficking

Cellular Transport & trafficking — doors, pumps and delivery vans

Two halves, one problem. A membrane is a wall that keeps compartments different; the cell then needs doors (transporters and channels) for small molecules and delivery vans (vesicles) for proteins. Every figure from the module, decoded, with the mechanism behind it and what breaks in disease.

Covers §2 Membrane transport (2.1, 2.2) · §3 Protein trafficking (3.1, 3.2) Figures 33 plates from the iLearn module Recall after every section

§0Membrane transport · introduction

Crossing the membrane

A barrier is only useful if you control the gaps in it.

Eukaryotic membranes are a phospholipid bilayer: hydrophilic polar heads face the water on each side, hydrophobic hydrocarbon tails hide in the middle and keep water out. The face toward the outside environment is the exoplasmic face; the face toward the cytosol is the cytosolic face. Organelle membranes have the same two faces, and the inside of an organelle (its lumen) is topologically equivalent to the outside of the cell. That point comes back in §3, because a vesicle's lumen stays "outside" the whole way.

The membrane is first a barrier. The plasma membrane stops the cell's contents mixing with the environment, and organelle membranes keep their proteins and solutes apart from the cytoplasm. Being separate is what lets each compartment hold different conditions: a concentration gradient, an acidic pH in a lysosome. A cell still has to import fuel and building blocks and export waste, so movement across a membrane has to be highly specific and tightly regulated. Whether a substance can cross depends on its chemistry (size, charge, polarity) and on how permeable the membrane is to it. Hydrophilic molecules and ions can't pass through the hydrophobic core, so membranes carry selective transporter and channel proteins that span the bilayer.

Reasoning · why compartments are worth the cost

Keeping things separate costs energy (pumps run constantly, see §1.5), but it buys different chemistry in different rooms. Lysosomal enzymes work at pH ~5 and would digest the cytosol if they leaked. A steep Na⁺ gradient across the plasma membrane is stored energy the cell spends to drive other transport (§1.3) and to fire nerves (§2.3). A gradient only exists if there is a wall to hold it, and the wall is the bilayer.

§0.1Simple diffusion — what the bare bilayer lets through

Diffusion is net movement from high to low concentration. It is simple when the molecule goes straight through the lipid bilayer, and facilitated when a transporter or channel protein carries it across. In simple diffusion across a protein-free bilayer, the rate depends on two things: how hydrophobic the molecule is and how small it is. Plate 0.1 (the module's drag-and-drop activity) ranks the four classes.

🤔 Predict · before you read on

Rank these by how easily they cross a pure lipid bilayer: Na⁺, glucose, water, O₂.

O₂ > water > glucose > Na⁺. O₂ is small and hydrophobic, so it dissolves in the lipid core and passes freely. Water is small and polar and leaks through slowly. Glucose is a large polar molecule and barely gets through. Na⁺ carries a charge and a shell of water, so the bilayer effectively blocks it.
Label Key — permeability by molecule class
Ions (red, bounces back)
Charged and surrounded by a hydration shell, so they cannot enter the hydrophobic core. This is why every ion needs a protein to cross, and why ion gradients can be held so steeply.
Large uncharged polar (thin yellow)
Glucose-sized polar molecules: most are turned back and only a trickle crosses. Cells that need lots of glucose therefore use transporters (§1.3).
Small uncharged polar (blue, partly through)
Water, urea, glycerol. These are small enough to slip through slowly. Water's slow leak is why some cells add aquaporins (§2.5).
Hydrophobic molecules (green, straight through)
O₂, CO₂, N₂, steroid hormones. They dissolve in the lipid core and cross freely, which is why gas exchange and steroid signalling need no transporter.
Lipid bilayer
The selective barrier itself. Its oily core is the filter that sorts these classes.
Clinical / real-world · drug design follows the same rule

Small, lipophilic, uncharged drugs cross membranes (gut wall, blood–brain barrier) by simple diffusion. Charged or very polar drugs mostly do not. That is why many drugs are formulated as weak acids or bases that are partly un-ionised at body pH, and why a quaternary-ammonium drug, which is permanently charged, stays out of the brain.

§0.2Facilitated diffusion — transporters vs channels

Membrane transport proteins let hydrophilic solutes cross without ever touching the hydrophobic interior. There are two kinds, shown side by side in Plate 0.2: transporters, which bind the solute and change shape to move it, and channels, which open a water-filled pore that solutes flow through.

Label Key — the two classes of transport protein
Transporters (⇄ two shapes)
The solute binds a specific site, and the protein flips conformation to expose it on the other side. Because it binds like an enzyme, it is highly selective, but it is slower since every cycle needs a shape change.
Channels (open pore)
A continuous pore. When open, solutes stream through with no shape change per ion, so channels are much faster. They select mainly by size and charge.

§0.3Passive vs active transport

All channels and many transporters let solutes cross spontaneously down their concentration gradient. This is passive transport, and it covers both simple and facilitated diffusion. Moving something against its gradient needs an input of energy, and this is active transport. Look at Plate 0.3: the "ENERGY" arrow attaches only to a transporter, never to a channel. A pore can't push anything uphill. All it can do is let solutes run downhill faster.

Label Key — direction and energy
Simple diffusion
Straight through the lipid, downhill, no protein. Limited to small or hydrophobic molecules (Plate 0.1).
Channel-mediated
Downhill through a pore. This is passive, so the gradient alone sets the direction.
Transporter-mediated
Downhill via a binding protein (e.g. GLUT glucose uniporters). Still passive.
Active transport + ENERGY
Uphill, against the gradient. The energy comes from ATP or from another solute's gradient (§1.2). Only transporters can do this.
Concentration gradient (grey arrow)
High → low. Passive transport runs with it; active transport runs against it.
Memory hook · "channels only go downhill"

A channel is a door; a transporter is a lift. Doors only let you walk downhill (passive). A lift can carry you up (active), but only if it is powered by ATP or by a second passenger walking down.

R Recall — crossing the membrane
  • Simple diffusion rate depends on — hydrophobicity and size
  • Freely permeable — small hydrophobic molecules (O₂, CO₂)
  • Essentially impermeable — ions
  • Two transport protein classes — transporters (bind + change shape) and channels (pore)
  • Passive transport moves — down the gradient
  • Active transport moves — against the gradient, needs energy
  • Active transport only by — transporters, never channels
§12.1 · Membrane transporter proteins

Transporter proteins

Bind, flip, release, and if powered, push uphill.

Transporters move only molecules or ions that fit a specific binding site, so they are highly selective and bind their solute the way an enzyme binds its substrate. When the solute binds, the transporter changes conformation and carries it across. Everything in this section is a variation on that one move.

§1.1Alternating access — the three states

A transporter cycles between three states, shown left to right in Plate 1.1:

  • Outward-open: the binding site faces the outside.
  • Occluded: the site is closed off from both sides.
  • Inward-open: the site faces the inside of the bilayer.

The flips between outward-open and inward-open happen spontaneously and randomly. So why is there net movement? When solute is concentrated outside, the site is more often loaded in the outward-open state than in the inward-open state. Each random flip therefore carries more solute in than out, and the result is net transport down the gradient: passive transport.

Label Key — the transport cycle
Outward-open
The site is open to the high-concentration side, so it is likely to be loaded.
Occluded
The safety lock. The site is never open to both sides at once, so the transporter can't act as a leaky pore. This is the key difference from a channel.
Inward-open
The site faces the low-concentration side, so the solute is likely to dissociate.
⇄ arrows
Every step is reversible. The gradient, not the protein, sets the net direction for a passive transporter.
Concentration gradient
High outside, low inside, so the net flux is inward.
Reasoning · why the occluded state matters

If a transporter could be open to both sides at once, it would be a channel, and an active pump would leak its hard-won gradient straight back. The occluded intermediate guarantees that the "door" on one side shuts before the other opens, the way an airlock does. That is what lets transporters (and only transporters) be coupled to energy and push uphill.

Active transporters

Active transport against the gradient keeps ion concentrations inside cells right and imports solutes that are scarcer outside than in. These transporters are pumps. The energy comes in one of two ways, compared in Plate 1.2: ATP hydrolysis, or a coupled transporter that spends one solute's downhill electrochemical gradient to drive another solute uphill.

Label Key — energy sources
Coupled transporter
Moves the uphill solute (red) only together with a downhill solute (orange). The orange solute's gradient pays the energy bill. This is secondary active transport.
ATP-driven pump
Hydrolyses ATP → ADP and becomes phosphorylated (P). The phosphorylation drives the shape change that moves the solute uphill. This is primary active transport.
Electrochemical gradient (orange arrow)
The downhill gradient that the coupled transporter spends. It was originally built by an ATP pump, so ATP pays for everything in the end.

§1.2Coupled transporters — uniport, symport, antiport

A coupled transporter links one solute's movement to another's. The electrochemical gradient of solute A moving down drives solute B against its own gradient. Plate 1.3 sorts the geometry:

  • Symporter: both solutes move in the same direction.
  • Antiporter: the two solutes move in opposite directions.
  • Uniporter: not coupled; it moves only one solute type (e.g. GLUT glucose uniporters, which are passive).
Label Key — transport geometry
Transported molecule (red)
The solute the cell actually wants to move.
Co-transported ion (blue)
Usually Na⁺ (or H⁺). Its downhill flow is the "currency" that pays for the red solute.
Uniport
One solute only, no coupling. It can only carry its solute downhill.
Symport
Same direction, e.g. Na⁺ and glucose both entering (§1.3).
Antiport
Opposite directions, e.g. the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger: Na⁺ in, Ca²⁺ out.
Coupled transport (bracket)
Symport and antiport are the coupled forms. The uniport sits outside the bracket.

§1.3Worked example of coupling — the Na⁺–glucose symporter

This symporter sits in the apical membrane of small-intestine epithelial cells. Na⁺ and glucose bind and are co-transported into the cell. Na⁺ moves down its electrochemical gradient, because intracellular Na⁺ is low. Glucose moves against its gradient, because it is already more concentrated inside the cell. The energy stored in the Na⁺ gradient drags glucose in. The steeper the Na⁺ gradient, the more Na⁺ enters and the more glucose comes with it.

Binding is cooperative: binding either solute raises the affinity for the other. Trace the cycle in Plate 1.4. Na⁺ binds in the outward-open state, and glucose then binds too. The protein reaches the occluded-occupied state only when both are bound, and then opens inward to release them.

Label Key — the five states
Occluded-empty
The resting state, closed to both sides.
Outward-open
Faces the gut lumen, where Na⁺ is high, so Na⁺ binds readily and raises the affinity for glucose.
Occluded-occupied
Reached only with both Na⁺ and glucose bound. This is the coupling rule: no Na⁺ means no glucose transport, so the protein can't leak glucose back or let Na⁺ through on its own.
Inward-open
Faces the cytosol, where Na⁺ is low, so Na⁺ falls off. Losing Na⁺ lowers the glucose affinity, and glucose is released even though cytosolic glucose is high.
Na⁺ electrochemical gradient (left)
Points inward. This is the energy source.
Glucose concentration gradient (right)
Points outward, higher inside. Glucose is being pushed uphill.
Reasoning · how cooperativity enforces coupling

The trick is the affinity switch. Outside, Na⁺ is abundant, so it binds and makes the site "sticky" for glucose. Inside, Na⁺ is scarce, so it leaves, the site loses its grip, and glucose drops off even against a high glucose concentration. Requiring both solutes for the occluded state means the protein never moves one without the other. Glucose uptake is literally paid for in Na⁺.

Clinical / real-world · oral rehydration and gliflozins

Oral rehydration solution (salt + glucose) works because this symporter pulls Na⁺ and glucose in together and water follows osmotically, even when diarrhoea (e.g. cholera) is flushing secretions out. Salt water or sugar water alone absorbs far less. A related symporter in the kidney tubule (SGLT2) reabsorbs filtered glucose, and blocking it with SGLT2 inhibitors (the "-gliflozins") makes the body excrete glucose in urine, which is a type 2 diabetes treatment.

§1.4ATPase pumps — the four types

ATP-driven pumps (ATPases) hydrolyse ATP to push a solute against its electrochemical gradient. There are four types, side by side in Plate 1.5.

Label Key — the four ATPase classes
P-type pump
Pumps ions (H⁺, K⁺, Na⁺, Ca²⁺) and phosphorylates itself during the cycle (the "P"). Examples: the Na⁺/K⁺ pump (§1.5), the Ca²⁺ pump of muscle SR, and the gastric H⁺/K⁺ pump.
ABC transporter
"ATP-Binding Cassette". Binds 2 ATP and pumps small molecules (drugs, lipids, peptides) across the membrane. ADP + Pᵢ are released after hydrolysis.
V-type proton pump
Uses ATP to pump H⁺ into organelles such as lysosomes and endosomes. This is how their lumen is acidified to pH ~5 (§5.1).
F-type ATP synthase
The same architecture running in reverse: H⁺ flowing down its gradient turns the rotor and makes ATP from ADP + Pᵢ. It sits in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
Reasoning · V-type and F-type are the same machine, run in opposite directions

Every transporter step is reversible (Plate 1.1). Spend ATP and the rotor pumps protons uphill (V-type). Supply a steep enough proton gradient and the same motor turns the other way, so the protons' fall synthesises ATP (F-type). Which way it runs depends on which store of energy is bigger, the ATP/ADP ratio or the H⁺ gradient.

Clinical / real-world · targets you'll meet again

Proton-pump inhibitors (omeprazole) block the gastric P-type H⁺/K⁺ ATPase to reduce stomach acid. ABC transporters such as P-glycoprotein (MDR1) pump chemotherapy drugs back out of cancer cells, causing multidrug resistance. CFTR, the protein defective in cystic fibrosis, is an ABC-family member that acts as a Cl⁻ channel (and see §4.1 for why the common CF mutation never reaches the membrane).

§1.5The Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump

The Na⁺/K⁺ pump is a P-type ATPase in the plasma membrane. ATP hydrolysis phosphorylates it, and the conformational change swaps 3 Na⁺ out for 2 K⁺ in, both against their gradients. Because more positive charge leaves than enters, the pump makes the inside more negative and so contributes to the membrane potential. Follow the arrows in Plate 1.6.

Label Key — the pump and its gradients
3 Na⁺ (out)
Pumped out against the Na⁺ gradient. This builds the inward Na⁺ gradient that symporters (§1.3) and action potentials (§2.3) spend.
2 K⁺ (in)
Pumped in against the K⁺ gradient. This keeps cytosolic K⁺ high (~140 mM) so that K⁺ leak channels can set the resting potential (§2.2).
P (phosphorylated aspartate)
The defining P-type feature. Phosphorylation and dephosphorylation flip the pump between its outward- and inward-facing forms.
ATP → ADP
One ATP per cycle. This pump uses a large share of a resting cell's ATP (much more in neurons).
Na⁺ / K⁺ electrochemical gradients
Na⁺'s points inward (it wants in), K⁺'s points outward (it wants out). The pump works against both.
Worked example · net charge moved by the pump

How much net charge does the pump move per ATP, and in which direction?

  1. Charge out per cycle: 3 Na⁺ × (+1) = +3.
  2. Charge in per cycle: 2 K⁺ × (+1) = +2.
  3. Net: +3 − 2 = +1 charge leaves the cell per ATP hydrolysed.
  4. Losing positive charge makes the inside more negative, so the pump is electrogenic and contributes directly (though modestly) to the negative resting potential. Its bigger contribution is indirect: it builds the K⁺ gradient that leak channels then use.

Answer: one net positive charge exported per ATP; the inside becomes more negative.

Clinical / real-world · digoxin

Digoxin partly inhibits the cardiac Na⁺/K⁺ pump. Intracellular Na⁺ rises, which weakens the Na⁺ gradient that a Na⁺/Ca²⁺ antiporter uses to export Ca²⁺. More Ca²⁺ stays in the cell and the heart contracts more strongly. A pump, an antiporter and a gradient explain a heart-failure drug. Hypokalaemia makes digoxin toxicity worse because K⁺ competes with digoxin for the pump.

Memory hook · "3 Sodiums Sail out, 2 Kings come in"

Three out, two in, one ATP. The number of Na⁺ is bigger and they leave, so the cell is left negative.

R Recall — transporters
  • Three transporter states — outward-open, occluded, inward-open
  • State switching is — spontaneous and random; the gradient sets net direction
  • Symport — same direction
  • Antiport — opposite directions
  • Uniporter — one solute, not coupled
  • SGLT location — apical membrane of small-intestine epithelium
  • SGLT binding is — cooperative; occluded state needs both Na⁺ and glucose
  • Four ATPases — P-type, ABC, V-type, F-type
  • F-type ATP synthase — uses H⁺ flow to make ATP
  • Na⁺/K⁺ pump — P-type; 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in per ATP
§22.2 · Channels

Channels

Fast, selective, gated pores, and the electrical life of the cell.

Channel proteins form transmembrane pores for the passive movement of small molecules down their electrochemical gradient. Most of a cell's channels are ion channels (Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺, Cl⁻), and they are ion-selective: each lets specific ions through and excludes others.

§2.1Selectivity and gating

Selectivity depends on the channel's diameter, shape and the charged amino acids that line the pore. Ion channels are narrow in places, so ions brush against the wall, and only ions of the right size and charge pass. In water an ion is surrounded by water molecules. It has to shed that hydration shell to pass single-file through the selectivity filter at the narrowest point. Plate 2.1 shows four channels each passing only its own ion.

Label Key — one channel, one ion
Na⁺ channel
Passes Na⁺ inward, down its gradient. This drives the action-potential upstroke.
Ca²⁺ channel
Passes Ca²⁺ inward. Ca²⁺ is kept ~10,000× lower in the cytosol, so a brief opening is a powerful signal (e.g. neurotransmitter release).
K⁺ channel (arrow out)
K⁺ leaves, down its gradient. This sets the resting potential and repolarises after a spike.
Cl⁻ channel
Passes the anion Cl⁻. Its role depends on the cell (e.g. CFTR in airway fluid secretion).
Reasoning · how a K⁺ channel rejects the smaller Na⁺

Being small isn't enough. The filter is lined with carbonyl oxygens spaced to "stand in" for the water molecules around a K⁺ ion exactly, so dehydration costs K⁺ nothing. Na⁺ is smaller and can't touch all those oxygens at once, so shedding its water shell is too costly and it stays out. Selectivity comes from paying back the dehydration energy for one ion only, not from a simple size sieve.

Gating

Channels flicker between open and closed: they open briefly to let ions through, then close. The opening is tied to a specific stimulus, so ion channels are gated, and they are classified by that stimulus. Open channels move ions much faster than transporters because nothing has to change shape for each ion. Plate 2.2 sets out the four gating types.

Label Key — four gating stimuli
Voltage-gated
Charged segments (+++) sense the membrane potential. When the inside becomes less negative (depolarisation), they move and open the pore. These are the Na⁺ and K⁺ channels of the action potential (§2.3).
Ligand-gated (extracellular ligand)
Opens when a molecule such as a neurotransmitter binds the outside face. Example: the nicotinic ACh receptor at the synapse (§2.4).
Ligand-gated (intracellular ligand)
Opens when a cytosolic messenger (e.g. Ca²⁺, cAMP/cGMP) binds the inside face. This links intracellular signalling to excitability.
Mechanically gated
Opens when the membrane is stretched or pressed: vibrations or pressure, as in hair cells of the ear and touch receptors.
Cytosol
Marks the inside, which tells you which face each ligand binds.
Memory hook · the module's self-check

"I open in response to vibrations or pressure" → mechanically gated. Ask what opens it: Volts, Ligands or Touch.

§2.2Ion channels help generate the membrane potential

Membranes are impermeable to inorganic ions, so the inside can hold ion concentrations different from the outside. Those differences create a membrane potential, with the inside more negative than the exterior. A membrane is at its resting membrane potential when cation and anion movements balance and the voltage stays unchanged. Changes in potential as ions flow through open channels are the basis of electrical signalling in nerve and muscle cells.

The negative resting potential depends mainly on the K⁺ gradient built by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, and on K⁺ leaving through K⁺ leak channels that randomly switch between open and closed. At rest the driving force on K⁺ is almost zero, even though K⁺ is far more concentrated inside. The concentrations behind this are in Plate 2.3.

Label Key — the numbers and the two forces
Na⁺: 5–15 mM in / 145 out
~10× higher outside, so both concentration and voltage push Na⁺ in. Open Na⁺ channels give a big inward rush.
K⁺: 140 in / 5 out
~28× higher inside, so concentration pushes K⁺ out while the negative inside pulls it back. At rest these nearly cancel.
Mg²⁺: 0.5 in / 1–2 out
Mostly bound inside. Free levels are low.
Ca²⁺: 10⁻⁴ in / 1–2 out
A ~10⁴-fold gradient. Opening a few Ca²⁺ channels causes a large relative change, which is why Ca²⁺ works as a signal.
H⁺: pH 7.2 in / 7.4 out
The cytosol is slightly more acidic.
Cl⁻: 5–15 in / 110 out
The main extracellular anion. Many cell anions are instead macromolecules (proteins, nucleic acids) that can't leave.
Concentration gradient (no membrane potential)
Only chemical drive, with arrow size set by the concentration difference.
Electrochemical gradient with membrane potential
Chemical + electrical drive combined. For a cation entering a negative cell they add (big arrow); for an anion they oppose (small arrow).
Reasoning · why K⁺ has almost no driving force at rest

Open K⁺ leak channels let K⁺ seep out down its concentration gradient. Each K⁺ that leaves takes away positive charge, so the inside becomes more negative and pulls K⁺ back. Very quickly the electrical pull equals the chemical push. That balance point is the K⁺ equilibrium potential, and the resting potential sits close to it because at rest the membrane is mostly permeable to K⁺. Hence "driving force almost zero, despite more K⁺ inside."

Worked example · where does the balance point sit? (Nernst, extension)

The Nernst equation (at 37 °C, for a +1 ion) gives the voltage where electrical pull equals chemical push: E = 61.5 mV × log₁₀([out]/[in]). Use Plate 2.3's values.

  1. K⁺: [out]/[in] = 5/140 = 0.0357.
  2. log₁₀(0.0357) = −1.45.
  3. EK = 61.5 × (−1.45) ≈ −89 mV. The resting potential (~−70 mV) sits close to this, which is the K⁺ dominance from the Reasoning box above.
  4. Na⁺ (taking 10 mM inside): 145/10 = 14.5; log₁₀(14.5) = 1.16; ENa = 61.5 × 1.16 ≈ +71 mV.
  5. Interpretation: at −70 mV, Na⁺ is ~140 mV from its equilibrium and has a huge inward drive. K⁺ is only ~20 mV from its equilibrium and has little drive.

Answer: EK ≈ −89 mV, ENa ≈ +71 mV. This is why opening Na⁺ channels sends the membrane sharply positive (Plate 2.4).

Clinical / real-world · potassium is the dangerous ion

Because the resting potential is set by the K⁺ gradient, changing plasma K⁺ shifts it directly. Hyperkalaemia (raised extracellular K⁺) shrinks the gradient and depolarises cells. Cardiac Na⁺ channels then inactivate, which can cause arrhythmia or arrest. That is why K⁺ is checked on every blood panel and why IV K⁺ is never given as a rapid bolus.

§2.3Voltage-gated channels generate action potentials

Excitable cells (neurons, myocytes) carry voltage-gated channels that generate action potentials. A spike is triggered by depolarisation, a shift of the membrane potential to less negative inside. Depolarisation opens voltage-gated Na⁺ channels. Na⁺ rushes in down its electrochemical gradient, which depolarises the membrane further and opens more Na⁺ channels: a positive feedback loop. When the local potential approaches the point where the net driving force on Na⁺ is near zero, Na⁺ channels close and voltage-gated K⁺ channels open, restoring the negative resting value. Match each phase to Plate 2.4.

Label Key — phases of the spike
−70 mV baseline
Resting potential, set by K⁺ leak (§2.2).
Sodium channels open (yellow)
The threshold is reached and the first Na⁺ channels open.
More sodium channels open (green)
Positive feedback gives the explosive upstroke towards +30 mV.
Sodium channels close
Inactivation at the peak stops the Na⁺ entry.
Potassium channels open (blue)
K⁺ leaves and repolarises the membrane.
Potassium channels close
They close slowly, so the potential briefly undershoots below −70 mV before recovering.
1 ms scale
The whole event takes about a millisecond.

The spike then travels. In Plate 2.5, Na⁺ entering (red curved arrows) depolarises the next patch of axon (blue), which opens its Na⁺ channels, and so on. The spike always moves away from where it started, because the Na⁺ channels just behind it are inactivated and can't reopen.

Label Key — why the spike is one-way
Na⁺ channels: Closed / Inactivated / Open / Closed
The three channel states along the axon. Inactivated is different from closed: the channel can't open again until the membrane repolarises.
Repolarised
The membrane behind the spike has recovered but its channels are still inactivated. This is the refractory zone.
Depolarised (blue)
The active region, where Na⁺ is entering.
Propagation →
Current spreads forward into resting membrane, whose channels can open.
Resting
Membrane ahead of the spike that is ready to fire.
t = 0 → t = 1 ms
The whole pattern has shifted along the axon.
Cell body, dendrites, axon, terminal branches
The neuron's anatomy. Axons run from <1 mm to >1 m, and the spike carries the signal the full length to the terminals.
Reasoning · inactivation is what gives the signal direction

Depolarising current spreads both ways from the active patch. If the membrane behind could fire again, the spike would bounce back and forth. Na⁺-channel inactivation makes the patch just fired refractory for a moment, so only the forward patch can respond. The same refractory period also caps how fast a neuron can fire.

Clinical / real-world · blocking the Na⁺ channel

Local anaesthetics (lidocaine) block voltage-gated Na⁺ channels, so no upstroke and no propagation: pain signals never reach the brain. Tetrodotoxin (pufferfish) blocks the same channel and causes paralysis. Several anti-epileptics (phenytoin, carbamazepine) stabilise the inactivated state to damp runaway firing.

§2.4At the synapse — voltage becomes chemistry and back

When an action potential reaches the nerve terminal, the terminal releases neurotransmitter. The transmitter binds ligand-gated ion channels on the postsynaptic cell and opens them. The resulting ion flow changes the postsynaptic membrane potential, and the signal has crossed. Plate 2.6 contrasts the resting and active synapse.

Label Key — parts of the synapse
Nerve terminal of presynaptic cell
Where the action potential arrives. Its voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open and trigger release.
Neurotransmitter in synaptic vesicle
Stored in vesicles and released by regulated exocytosis (§4.5) when the signal arrives.
Synaptic cleft
The narrow gap the transmitter diffuses across.
Transmitter-gated ion channel
An extracellular-ligand-gated channel (Plate 2.2) that turns the chemical signal back into an ion current.
Postsynaptic target cell / target cell plasma membrane
Its potential shifts when the channels open.
Resting vs active
Closed channels with no release, versus vesicles fusing and channels opening.
Clinical / real-world · myasthenia gravis

In myasthenia gravis, autoantibodies attack the transmitter-gated ACh receptor channel at the neuromuscular junction. Fewer working channels give a smaller postsynaptic response, so muscles tire with repeated use. Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors help by leaving more ACh in the cleft for the channels that remain.

§2.5Aquaporins

Water crosses membranes passively down its own concentration gradient, which is osmosis. Water is small, uncharged and polar, so it can diffuse through the bilayer directly, but only slowly (Plate 0.1). Cells that need fast water flow add channel proteins called aquaporins. These are built to pass uncharged water while blocking ions, the exact opposite of ion channels, which pass ions and block water. Plate 2.7 shows them at work in a secretory gland.

Label Key — secreting fluid
Ion pumps and channels (red dots)
Move ions into the lumen first, creating an osmotic gradient.
Aquaporins (green dots)
Let water follow the ions rapidly. Without them, secretion would be limited by the slow bilayer leak.
Ions (red arrow) → water (green arrow)
The order matters: the ions go first and water follows osmotically.
Apical membrane
Faces the lumen, where the secretion leaves.
Basolateral membrane
Faces the blood or tissue side, where water and ions are drawn in.
Duct → fluid
The secreted fluid drains away (e.g. saliva, sweat).
Clinical / real-world · nephrogenic diabetes insipidus

In the kidney collecting duct, ADH (vasopressin) inserts aquaporin-2 into the apical membrane so water is reabsorbed. Mutations in AQP2 or its receptor mean the duct can't take water back, so the patient passes large volumes of dilute urine whatever their ADH level. Notice too that the inserted channels are delivered by regulated vesicle traffic, which leads into §3.

R Recall — channels
  • Channel transport is — passive, down the electrochemical gradient
  • Selectivity depends on — diameter, shape, charged lining residues
  • To pass the filter, ions must — shed their water shell
  • Four gating types — voltage, extracellular ligand, intracellular ligand, mechanical
  • Channels faster than transporters because — no conformational change per ion
  • Resting potential set mainly by — K⁺ leak channels and the K⁺ gradient
  • K⁺: inside / outside — 140 mM / 5 mM
  • AP upstroke — voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open (positive feedback)
  • Repolarisation — Na⁺ channels close, K⁺ channels open
  • One-way propagation due to — Na⁺-channel inactivation
  • Aquaporins pass — water and block ions
§33 · Protein trafficking

Vesicular transport

Proteins are too big for doors, so they travel by van.

Proteins move between organelles in three ways: through pores (e.g. nuclear pores), through translocator proteins (e.g. into the ER or mitochondria), or by vesicular transport. Movement from the ER to the plasma membrane, and from the plasma membrane to lysosomes, all uses vesicles.

Vesicles are small, spherical, membrane-bound containers that collect cargo (e.g. proteins) and carry it between compartments. They are selective twice: about their contents (which cargo gets loaded) and about their destination (which membrane they fuse with). That is the delivery-van analogy in Plate 3.1.

Label Key — the analogy
Vesicle (lipid sphere = van)
A bilayer bubble. Its lumen is topologically "outside", so luminal cargo never touches the cytosol.
Cargo (red dots and green receptors = parcels)
Soluble proteins inside, plus membrane proteins (green) spanning the vesicle wall. Both are chosen deliberately.

§3.1The traffic map — organised and directional

Vesicle traffic links many organelles, but each route is highly specific. Organelles use vesicles to communicate with each other and with the cell exterior. Plate 3.2 is the master map, colour-coded into three streams.

Label Key — reading the map
Secretory pathway (red)
ER → Golgi → plasma membrane, or → (via endosomes) lysosomes. This is how new proteins go outward (§4).
Endocytic pathway (green)
Plasma membrane → endocytic vesicles → early endosomes → (via late endosomes) lysosomes. This is how material comes in (§5).
Retrieval pathways (blue)
Recovery routes. Early endosome → cell surface (some via recycling endosomes); endosomes → Golgi; Golgi → ER. They return receptors, membrane and escaped proteins.
Cytosol vs extracellular space (A)
Every arrow crosses between compartments by vesicle; cargo in the lumen never enters the cytosol.
Nuclear envelope, ER, Golgi cisternae (B)
The start of the secretory route. The ER is continuous with the nuclear envelope.
Early / late / recycling endosome, lysosome
The sorting stations and the final degradative compartment of the endocytic route.
Secretory vesicle
The end point of the secretory route at the plasma membrane.
Reasoning · why retrieval is essential

Every forward vesicle carries away a patch of the donor's membrane and its machinery (receptors, SNAREs). Without return traffic, the ER would shrink, the plasma membrane would swell, and the donor would run out of the proteins that make vesicles. Retrieval (blue) is the cell keeping its membrane and machinery in balance, not a minor side-route.

§3.2Principles — budding, coats and fusion

The basic cycle in Plate 3.3: a cargo-loaded vesicle buds off a donor organelle, travels through the cytosol, and fuses with a target organelle, releasing its cargo into the target lumen.

Label Key — one round trip
Donor compartment / lumen
The source. Its lumen contents become the vesicle contents.
Cargo molecules (with receptors)
Gathered at the bud site. Cargo that isn't selected stays behind.
Budding
The membrane curves and pinches off with the cargo.
Cytosol
The vesicle travels here. Only its outer, cytosolic face is exposed.
Fusion
The vesicle and target membranes merge.
Target compartment
Cargo ends up in its lumen, and the vesicle membrane becomes part of the target's membrane.

Most vesicles form at special patches of membrane carrying coat proteins, and a budding vesicle wears a distinctive coat on its outer surface. The steps, left to right in Plate 3.4:

  1. Coat assembly and cargo selection. Coat-recruitment (adaptor) proteins span the membrane: on the inner face they bind cargo receptors and gather them together, and on the cytosolic face they bind coat proteins. Cargo carries specific transport signals that cargo receptors recognise.
  2. Bud formation. On the outer layer, coat proteins assemble into a curved lattice that bends the membrane into a coated bud (a coated pit at the plasma membrane).
  3. Vesicle formation. Dynamin, a membrane-bending GTPase, is recruited to the bud neck and constricts it, pinching the vesicle off.
  4. Uncoating. The outer coat is lost soon after budding. The cytosolic face has to be bare because fusion needs the two membranes to come very close.
Label Key — the coated-vesicle cycle
Donor membrane / cargo receptor / cargo molecules
Receptors in the membrane hold the cargo on the luminal side.
Adaptor protein
Links cargo receptors to the coat. It is the selection step that decides what gets packed.
Clathrin triskelion
A three-legged clathrin unit. Many of them interlock into the curved cage that shapes the bud.
Membrane-bending and fission proteins
Dynamin and partners at the neck that constrict and cut it.
Coated vesicle membrane
The free vesicle, still in its cage.
Naked transport vesicle
After uncoating, with the coat components recycled (top right), and ready to dock and fuse.
Long arrows
Coat proteins return to the cytosol and are reused for the next bud.
Clinical / real-world · dynamin

Mutations in dynamin-2 cause centronuclear myopathy and a form of Charcot–Marie–Tooth neuropathy. In both, cells that depend on heavy membrane turnover (muscle, and nerve terminals that recycle synaptic vesicles constantly) can't pinch vesicles off efficiently.

§3.3Three coats for three kinds of step

Vesicles fall into three main types according to their coat. Plate 3.5 colour-codes where each one works:

  • Clathrin: transport from the Golgi (trans-Golgi network) and from the plasma membrane.
  • COPI: Golgi → ER, the retrograde (backward) direction.
  • COPII: ER → Golgi cisternae, the anterograde (forward) direction.
Label Key — coats by location
COPII (red) on the ER
Forward from the ER, carrying new proteins out.
COPI (blue) on the Golgi cisternae
Backward, from Golgi to ER and between cisternae, retrieving escaped ER proteins (§4.2).
Clathrin (green) at the trans-Golgi network and plasma membrane
TGN → endosomes (lysosomal cargo), and the plasma membrane → early endosome (endocytosis).
Golgi cisternae, trans Golgi network, Golgi apparatus
The processing stack between ER and destinations.
Late / early endosome, secretory vesicle
Destinations and sources of clathrin traffic and secretion.
Extracellular space / cytosol / plasma membrane
Topology: buds always form into the cytosol.
Memory hook · "COPII goes Up; COPI comes back"

COPII = two = to the Golgi (forward). COPI = I return (back to the ER). Clathrin works at the two ends: the trans-Golgi and the cell surface.

§3.4Coat assembly is switched on by GTPases

Traffic in and out of each organelle has to stay balanced, so coats should assemble only when and where needed. Coat-recruitment GTPases control this. They sit in the cytosol at high concentration in their inactive GDP-bound state until called. There are two to know:

  • ARF: assembles COPI and clathrin coats at Golgi membranes.
  • Sar1: assembles COPII coats at the ER membrane.

Plate 3.6 (Table 14-1) puts every vesicle type, step, coat and GTPase in one grid.

Label Key — decoding the table
COPII · ER → cis-Golgi
Coat: Sec23/Sec24 + Sec13/Sec31 complexes, Sec16. GTPase: Sar1.
COPI · cis-Golgi → ER; later → earlier cisternae
Coat: coatomers of seven different COP subunits. GTPase: ARF.
Clathrin + AP1 · trans-Golgi → endosome
Lysosomal-enzyme delivery (§4.4). ARF.
Clathrin + GGA · trans-Golgi → endosome
A second adaptor for the same route. ARF.
Clathrin + AP2 · plasma membrane → endosome
Endocytosis (§5.3, LDL). ARF.
AP3 · Golgi → lysosome, melanosome, platelet vesicles
Specialised lysosome-related organelles. ARF. (Footnote: each AP complex has four different subunits, and it is not known whether AP3 coats contain clathrin.)
Pattern to notice
Sar1 for COPII only; ARF for everything else.

GTPases as molecular switches

Monomeric GTPases hydrolyse GTP and act as molecular switches: GTP-bound = ON (active), GDP-bound = OFF (inactive). In Plate 3.7A, hydrolysis turns the switch off, and resetting it requires GDP to leave slowly and GTP to bind fast. Plate 3.7B adds the regulators: GEFs (guanine-nucleotide exchange factors) promote GTP binding and switch it ON; GAPs (GTPase-activating proteins) promote hydrolysis and switch it OFF.

Label Key — the switch
GTP — ON / active
The protein's shape lets it bind effectors (for Sar1, the coat proteins).
GTP hydrolysis → GDP + Pᵢ — OFF / inactive
A built-in timer. The intrinsic hydrolysis is slow; GAP speeds it up.
Slow GDP release, fast GTP binding
Release of GDP is the rate-limiting step, so the switch stays OFF until a GEF pries GDP out.
Signal in → GEF
The input that turns the switch ON.
GAP → Pᵢ
Turns the switch OFF.
Signal out
What the active GTPase does, e.g. recruit a coat.
Reasoning · why build traffic on a timer switch?

A GTPase is a switch that resets itself: once on, it will turn itself off. That gives where control (the GEF sits only on the right membrane, e.g. Sar1-GEF on the ER) and when control (hydrolysis ends the job, so coats come off and vesicles can fuse). The same switch logic runs Rabs (§3.5) and the Ras signalling you'll meet in Week 11.

Assembly of a COPII vesicle by Sar1

Put it together in Plate 3.8, read left to right:

  1. Inactive, soluble Sar1-GDP meets Sar1-GEF, which sits in the ER membrane. GDP is swapped for GTP.
  2. Active Sar1-GTP exposes an amphiphilic helix that inserts into the cytosolic leaflet of the ER membrane. This anchors Sar1 and starts bending the membrane.
  3. Membrane-bound Sar1-GTP recruits the inner coat, Sec23/Sec24. Sec24 binds cargo receptors, which hold the luminal cargo.
  4. The outer coat, Sec13/31, assembles over the top and shapes a COPII-coated vesicle around the selected membrane proteins.
Label Key — COPII parts
Inactive, soluble Sar1-GDP
Floats free in the cytosol and is harmless until activated.
Sar1-GEF (ER membrane)
Restricts activation to the ER, so COPII buds only form there.
Active, membrane-bound Sar1-GTP · amphiphilic helix
The GTP-triggered helix is both anchor and wedge: it inserts into one leaflet and starts curving the membrane.
Donor membrane (ER) / ER lumen / cytosol
The coat assembles on the cytosolic face while cargo sits in the lumen.
Sec23 / Sec24
Inner coat. Sec24 is the cargo-selecting adaptor.
Cargo receptor · cargo
Links the luminal cargo to the coat, across the membrane.
Sec13/31 · outer coat / inner coat
The outer lattice that finishes the curvature.
Selected membrane proteins
Only these are packed in, which is the selectivity step.
COPII-coated vesicle / COPII vesicle
The finished product leaving for the cis-Golgi.

§3.5Finding the right address — Rabs and SNAREs

Vesicles must recognise the correct target membrane. Every transport vesicle carries surface markers that show its origin and cargo, and complementary receptors on the target recognise them. Rab proteins are GTPases on both vesicles and target membranes that help guide vesicles to the right place. Rabs dock; SNAREs fuse. The sequence in Plate 3.9:

  1. Tethering. A Rab effector (tethering protein) and an active Rab-GTP bind each other across the gap, making the first connection between the two membranes.
  2. Docking. SNAREs on the two membranes (v-SNARE on the vesicle, t-SNARE on the target) interact and wind together into a trans-SNARE complex that holds the vesicle tight against the target. SNARE pairing is highly specific.
  3. Fusion. When the two bilayers come within <1.5 nm, lipids flow from one to the other and they fuse.
  4. Reset. During docking and fusion, a Rab-GAP makes Rab hydrolyse its GTP. Rab-GDP leaves the membrane and returns to the cytosol, inactive (held there by GDI).
Label Key — targeting and fusion
Cargo receptor / cargo
Still on board from budding.
Rab-GTP
The active address marker. Different Rabs label different compartments.
Rab effector (tethering protein)
A long tether on the target that catches the vesicle at a distance. This gives tethering.
v-SNARE (red) / t-SNARE (blue)
Vesicle and target SNAREs. Only matching pairs zip, which gives a second check on the address.
Trans-SNARE complex (boxed)
The zipped four-helix bundle that pulls the membranes together. The energy of zipping drives fusion.
Rab-GDP + GDI
The spent Rab, extracted from the membrane by GDI and recycled.
Cytosol / target membrane
Fusion opens the vesicle lumen into the target lumen.
Inset: water displaced → form stalk → hemifusion → fusion
The SNAREs squeeze out the water between the membranes. The cytosolic leaflets merge first (stalk, then hemifusion), then the non-cytosolic leaflets, opening a fusion pore. Scale bar 10 nm.
Reasoning · two independent checks make delivery accurate

Rabs and SNAREs each carry address information, and both must match. Rab + tether is a long-range "is this the right building?" check; v-SNARE/t-SNARE pairing is a close-range "is this the right door?" check. Requiring both makes mis-delivery rare. Uncoating (§3.2) has to happen first, because the coat would keep the bilayers too far apart for the <1.5 nm contact.

Clinical / real-world · toxins that cut SNAREs

Botulinum and tetanus toxins are proteases that cleave neuronal SNAREs. Synaptic vesicles can't fuse, so neurotransmitter isn't released. Botulinum blocks ACh release at the neuromuscular junction, giving flaccid paralysis (and therapeutic "Botox"). Tetanus blocks inhibitory interneurons, giving spastic paralysis. The protein target is the same; the different symptoms come from different neurons being affected.

R Recall — vesicular transport
  • Vesicles are selective for — cargo and target membrane
  • Three pathways — secretory (red), endocytic (green), retrieval (blue)
  • Adaptor/coat-recruitment proteins — bind cargo receptors inside, coat proteins outside
  • Pinches the vesicle neck — dynamin (a GTPase)
  • Why uncoat before fusion — membranes must closely interact
  • COPII — ER → Golgi, anterograde
  • COPI — Golgi → ER, retrograde
  • Clathrin — from the Golgi and the plasma membrane
  • Sar1 assembles — COPII at the ER
  • ARF assembles — COPI and clathrin at the Golgi
  • GEF — promotes GTP binding (ON)
  • GAP — promotes hydrolysis (OFF)
  • Rabs — tether/dock vesicles
  • SNAREs — catalyse fusion
  • Lipid fusion distance — <1.5 nm
§43.1 · Secretory pathways

The secretory pathway

ER → Golgi → destination, with quality control at every gate.

Moving a protein from one organelle to the next balances forward and backward (retrieval) pathways. Getting to the surface takes many steps of collecting and dispatching. This section follows the outward path: made and modified in the ER, modified and sorted in the Golgi, then out to the plasma membrane and beyond. Plate 4.1 highlights the route.

Label Key — the outward path
ER ⇄ Golgi (red/blue double arrow)
Forward traffic (COPII) with retrieval (COPI) running alongside.
Golgi → secretory vesicles → cell exterior
The regulated route (stored, then released on signal).
Golgi → cell exterior (direct red arrow)
The constitutive route (continuous) (§4.5).
Late/early/recycling endosome, lysosome (white)
Not highlighted here. These are the endocytic and lysosomal branches (§4.4, §5).

§4.1Processing and quality control in the ER

Most proteins are chemically modified in the ER, chiefly by glycosylation, the attachment of short oligosaccharide side chains. These sugars protect the protein from degradation, hold it in the ER until it is properly folded, or act as a transport signal that helps route it to the right organelle.

Leaving the ER is highly selective and depends on correct folding. Misfolded proteins are kept in the ER and bound by chaperones that help them fold. If a protein still can't fold correctly, it is exported to the cytosol and degraded (by the proteasome, as in the Week 7 proteins material).

Reasoning · why check quality at the start

A misfolded secreted or membrane protein is useless at best and toxic at worst (aggregates, wrong activity). Checking at the very first gate is cheapest: the cell hasn't yet spent energy shipping and modifying the protein. The sugar tags serve as a progress flag the chaperones read, and a protein is held until folding is complete.

Clinical / real-world · cystic fibrosis ΔF508

The commonest CF mutation, ΔF508-CFTR, makes a Cl⁻ channel that could still partly work, but it misfolds, so ER quality control holds it and sends it for degradation. It never reaches the apical membrane. Modern "corrector" drugs (e.g. elexacaftor/tezacaftor) help it fold well enough to pass the ER checkpoint. The disease comes from the gatekeeping as much as from the protein's function. Similarly, α1-antitrypsin deficiency (Z variant) aggregates in hepatocyte ER, causing liver damage and lung emphysema from the missing secreted protein.

§4.2Leaving the ER — only correctly folded proteins

Secretory proteins start their journey packed into COPII-coated vesicles. Once these have budded and shed their coats, they fuse with one another into vesicular tubular clusters. The clusters are separate from the ER and contain no other ER proteins. They travel along microtubule tracks to the Golgi and fuse with the cis Golgi network.

ER-resident proteins sometimes escape into the clusters and get as far as the Golgi. They are sent back by retrograde transport in COPI vesicles. Plate 4.2 shows both directions together:

  • Anterograde (forward) transport by COPII vesicles (red), ER → Golgi, carrying newly made secretory or transmembrane proteins.
  • Retrograde (reverse) transport by COPI vesicles (blue), recycling membrane lipids and proteins such as SNAREs, and returning escaped ER residents.
Label Key — the ER–Golgi shuttle
Secretory protein (yellow)
Forward cargo heading out.
COPII coat · forward pathway
Anterograde vesicles leaving the ER.
Vesicular tubular cluster
Fused, uncoated COPII vesicles moving on microtubules to the cis-Golgi. It is also the first place escaped ER proteins are caught.
Soluble ER resident protein (red)
A protein that belongs in the ER (e.g. a chaperone) but leaked forward in bulk flow.
KDEL receptor protein (green)
Binds the KDEL retrieval signal (Lys-Asp-Glu-Leu) at the C-terminus of soluble ER residents in the clusters and Golgi, and carries them back.
COPI coat · retrieval pathway (blue)
Returns the KDEL receptor with its cargo to the ER.
cis Golgi network → cis, medial, trans cisternae → trans Golgi network
The Golgi compartments that cargo passes through (§4.3).
Reasoning · retrieve rather than hold back

Holding every chaperone perfectly in the ER would mean screening each COPII vesicle exactly. It is simpler to let bulk flow carry some out and fish them back with a receptor that recognises a tag (KDEL). The receptor binds more tightly in the slightly more acidic Golgi and releases its cargo back in the ER, so the pH difference between compartments sets the direction.

§4.3Movement through the Golgi apparatus

The Golgi is an ordered set of flattened, membrane-enclosed sacs (cisternae) arranged in stacks. Each stack has two faces: an entry cis face next to the ER and an exit trans face pointing to the plasma membrane. ER-derived vesicles with soluble proteins enter the cis Golgi network and move through the cisternae in vesicles that bud from one cisterna and fuse with the next. Along the way the proteins' oligosaccharide chains are modified step by step. At the trans Golgi network they are sorted by destination and leave in Golgi-derived vesicles. The order of modifications is in Plate 4.3.

Label Key — an assembly line, cis → trans
ER → cis Golgi network · SORTING
The entry checkpoint, where escaped ER residents are sent back (Plate 4.2).
Phosphorylation of oligosaccharides on lysosomal proteins (cis Golgi network)
Creates the mannose-6-phosphate (M6P) tag that later sends these proteins to lysosomes (§4.4).
Removal of Man (cis cisterna)
Trimming mannose residues added in the ER.
Removal of Man · addition of GlcNAc (medial cisterna)
Further trimming, then building with N-acetylglucosamine.
Addition of Gal · addition of NANA (trans cisterna)
Galactose and sialic acid (NANA) cap the chains, giving mature "complex" glycans.
Sulfation of tyrosines and carbohydrates (trans Golgi network)
The final modification before sorting.
SORTING → lysosome / plasma membrane / secretory vesicle
The exit sort into the three destinations.
Golgi stack vs Golgi apparatus
The stack is the cisternae; the apparatus includes the cis and trans networks at each end.
Reasoning · why put the enzymes in sequence

Each enzyme works on the product of the one before. Mannose has to be trimmed before GlcNAc can be added, and GlcNAc has to be added before galactose. Putting the enzymes in successive cisternae makes the modifications happen in the right order automatically, like stations on an assembly line. The same layout means a glycan's structure records how far its protein has travelled.

§4.4From the trans Golgi to the lysosome

Sorting to the lysosome is the best-understood example. New lysosomal proteins go from the ER lumen through the Golgi and leave the trans Golgi network in clathrin-coated vesicles (the module calls these endosomes), then travel on to lysosomes. In Plate 4.4 that is the Golgi → late endosome → lysosome arm. Endosome formation and maturation is covered in §5.

Label Key — the lysosomal branch
Golgi → (red/blue) → early endosome
Newly made lysosomal enzymes leave the TGN in clathrin/AP1 vesicles. The blue half of the arrow is receptor retrieval back to the Golgi.
Late endosome → lysosome (red/green)
Delivery into the degradative compartment, shared by the secretory (red) and endocytic (green) routes.
Early endosome ⇄ cell exterior (green/blue)
Endocytosis in, recycling out.
Recycling endosome (blue)
Returns receptors and membrane to the surface.
Secretory vesicles (white)
The separate route out to the exterior.
Clinical / real-world · I-cell disease

If the enzyme that adds the M6P tag in the cis Golgi (Plate 4.3, first step) is missing, lysosomal enzymes are never sorted to lysosomes. They are secreted into the blood by default. Lysosomes fill with undigested material, seen as "inclusion" bodies (I-cells), causing severe developmental and skeletal disease and early death. A single missing phosphate address label sends a whole class of proteins to the wrong place.

§4.5Exocytosis — constitutive vs regulated

Vesicles bound for the plasma membrane leave the trans Golgi network and fuse with it. This is exocytosis, and it provides new plasma-membrane components and secretes soluble proteins into the extracellular space. Depending on cell type there are two secretory pathways, shown in Plate 4.5:

  • Constitutive: in all cells, running continuously. It secretes many soluble proteins and also supplies the plasma membrane with newly made lipids and proteins.
  • Regulated: only in specialised secretory cells. Soluble proteins and other substances are stored in secretory vesicles and released only when an extracellular signal stimulates them. Hormones, neurotransmitters and digestive enzymes often leave this way.
Label Key — two exits
Newly synthesised soluble proteins for constitutive secretion (blue)
Leave continuously, e.g. extracellular matrix proteins, antibodies from plasma cells.
Newly synthesised plasma membrane lipids / protein
Carried in the vesicle membrane and added to the surface on fusion. This is membrane growth and renewal.
Unregulated membrane fusion → constitutive secretory pathway
No signal needed.
Secretory vesicle storing secretory proteins (red)
Concentrated, densely packed stores waiting at the membrane.
Signal such as hormone or neurotransmitter → intracellular signalling pathway
The trigger, often a rise in cytosolic Ca²⁺, which releases the brake on fusion.
Regulated membrane fusion → regulated secretory pathway
Release of a burst on demand.
Trans Golgi network / Golgi apparatus
Where cargo is sorted into the two routes.
Reasoning · why store instead of secrete continuously

Some products are needed in large amounts at a precise moment: insulin after a meal, neurotransmitter within a millisecond of a spike, digestive enzymes when food arrives. Making protein takes minutes to hours, which is far too slow. Pre-made, concentrated stores waiting at the membrane let the cell respond in seconds, as soon as the signal arrives.

Clinical / real-world · insulin secretion

Pancreatic β-cells store insulin in regulated secretory granules. Rising glucose raises cytosolic Ca²⁺, which triggers granule fusion. Sulfonylurea drugs push this same trigger. In type 2 diabetes the first, fast phase of release (from granules already docked) is typically the first to be lost.

R Recall — secretory pathway
  • Main ER modification — glycosylation (oligosaccharide side chains)
  • ER exit depends on — correct folding; failures → cytosol, degraded
  • Fused COPII vesicles form — vesicular tubular clusters, travel on microtubules
  • Escaped ER residents returned by — COPI vesicles (retrograde)
  • Golgi entry face — cis
  • Golgi exit face — trans
  • Sorting by destination happens at — the trans Golgi network
  • Lysosomal proteins leave the TGN in — clathrin-coated vesicles
  • Constitutive secretion — all cells, continuous
  • Regulated secretion — specialised cells, stored until a signal
§53.2 · Endocytosis

Endocytosis

Bringing the outside in, then sorting it to recycle or to destroy.

Endocytosis is how cells take substances from outside and bring them in. The cargo can be receptor–ligand complexes, nutrients, extracellular matrix, cell debris, bacteria and viruses, or even whole cells. A small patch of plasma membrane progressively encloses the material, first invaginating and then pinching off to form a vesicle. When the vesicles form at the plasma membrane and take in fluid, the process is pinocytosis ("cell drinking").

Cells constantly ingest pieces of their plasma membrane as small pinocytic vesicles. The rate is high, yet the surface area stays the same. So the same amount of membrane removed by endocytosis must be added back by exocytosis. The coupling is especially tight in cells with high turnover such as nerve terminals. The endocytic route is the green-arrow path on the map in Plate 4.4.

Reasoning · endo- and exocytosis are one membrane loop

If a cell internalises the equivalent of its whole surface every hour or so and stays the same size, membrane must be flowing in a loop: out by exocytosis (§4.5), in by endocytosis, and back via recycling endosomes. A synaptic terminal is the extreme case. Each vesicle fused at release has to be retrieved by endocytosis, or the terminal runs out of vesicles and the membrane balloons.

§5.1Vesicle formation and endosome maturation

It starts at clathrin-coated pits. Within about a minute a pit invaginates and pinches off as a clathrin-coated vesicle. The vesicle sheds its coat and fuses with an early endosome, where the cargo is sorted. Some cargo returns to the plasma membrane via a recycling endosome (blue arrows in Plate 5.1).

As the early endosome moves from the cell periphery towards the nucleus along microtubules (green line), it matures into a late endosome. In the process its membrane protein composition changes: it stops recycling material to the surface and commits what remains to degradation. Late endosomes fuse with each other and with lysosomes to form endolysosomes, which degrade their contents.

Label Key — maturation step by step
Plasma membrane → early endosome (black arrows)
Incoming endocytic vesicles deliver to the peripheral sorting station.
Recycling endosome (blue arrows)
Sends receptors and membrane back to the surface. Most of the internalised membrane is recycled this way.
Multivesicular body · intralumenal vesicles
The maturing endosome buds membrane inward, sealing proteins destined for destruction (e.g. activated receptors) inside internal vesicles so they can be digested whole.
Microtubule-mediated transport
Carries the maturing endosome inward towards the nucleus.
Late endosome · fusion
The committed, more acidic compartment. It no longer recycles.
Lysosome ⇄ endolysosome
Fusion forms the endolysosome where digestion happens. It then matures back into a lysosome (§5.2).
Trans Golgi network (black two-way arrows)
Delivers new lysosomal enzymes into endosomes and retrieves their receptors (§4.4).
Cytosol
All of this happens inside membrane-bounded lumens, so digestion never touches the cytosol.
Reasoning · falling pH drives the sorting

V-type proton pumps (§1.4) acidify each compartment more than the last: early endosome ~pH 6, late endosome ~5.5, lysosome ~5. Many receptors release their ligand at low pH, so cargo falls off in the early endosome and the empty receptor can be recycled. Lysosomal enzymes are acid hydrolases that only work well at the end of the line. The gradual drop in pH is what sorts and times the whole pathway.

§5.2Lysosomes — where traffic streams converge

A lysosome forms once most of the endocytosed material in an endolysosome has been digested and only resistant or slowly digestible residues remain. Lysosomes are meeting points where several streams of traffic converge. Four pathways feed material in for digestion, and Plate 5.2 draws all four:

  1. Endocytosis: uptake of macromolecules from extracellular fluid in vesicles.
  2. Phagocytosis: uptake of large particles and microorganisms by macrophages and neutrophils.
  3. Macropinocytosis: nonspecific uptake of fluid, membrane and particles attached to the plasma membrane.
  4. Autophagy: self-digestion of the cell's own cytosol and worn-out organelles.
Label Key — the four feeders
Bacterium → phagocytosis → phagosome
Large particle engulfed by an extending membrane. The phagosome then fuses with lysosomes to kill and digest it.
Endocytosis → early endosome → late endosome
Small vesicles, often receptor-mediated (§5.3).
Macropinocytosis
Large, nonspecific gulps of fluid and membrane.
Mitochondrion → autophagy → autophagosome
A double membrane wraps a worn-out organelle from inside the cell and delivers it for recycling.
Lysosome (centre right)
Where all four converge. It holds acid hydrolases at ~pH 5.
Extracellular fluid / cytosol / plasma membrane
Three routes start outside (from the extracellular fluid); autophagy alone starts inside (from the cytosol).
Clinical / real-world · when lysosomes can't finish the job

Lysosomal storage diseases (e.g. Tay–Sachs, Gaucher, Pompe) each lack one acid hydrolase, so its substrate builds up in lysosomes. Neurons, which can't dilute it by dividing, are hit hardest. Some pathogens escape this route: Mycobacterium tuberculosis stops its phagosome fusing with lysosomes, which is how it survives inside macrophages. Defective autophagy is linked to neurodegeneration and Crohn's disease.

§5.3Receptor-mediated endocytosis — LDL

Cholesterol travels in the blood as low-density lipoprotein (LDL) particles: a phospholipid monolayer around a cholesterol core, wrapped by one ApoB protein. Follow the numbered steps in Plate 5.3:

  1. LDL receptors on the cell surface bind ApoB and gather in clathrin-coated pits, attached via the AP2 adaptor complex (Plate 3.6: clathrin + AP2 = plasma membrane → endosome).
  2. The pit pinches off as a coated vesicle, which then uncoats.
  3. The vesicle fuses with an early endosome. As it matures into a late endosome (pH ~5), the acidity makes the receptor release its LDL.
  4. The free LDL is carried on to the lysosome, where it is broken down into amino acids (from ApoB), fatty acids and free cholesterol for the cell to use.
  5. The empty receptors bud off in vesicles and recycle to the plasma membrane. At neutral pH the ligand-binding arm is free to bind another LDL particle.
Label Key — the LDL cycle
LDL particle · phospholipid monolayer · ApoB protein
The cargo. ApoB is the part the receptor actually recognises.
LDL receptor
A transmembrane receptor whose cytoplasmic tail carries the signal that AP2 binds, so it is concentrated in pits.
Coated pit · clathrin · AP2 complex
AP2 is the adaptor connecting the receptor tail to the clathrin cage (Plate 3.4 in action).
Coated vesicle (1–2)
Internalised and then uncoated.
Early endosome → late endosome, pH 5.0 (3)
The acid pH separates receptor from LDL, the sorting decision of §5.1.
Lysosome · amino acids, fatty acids, cholesterol (4)
Digestion releases cholesterol for membranes and steroid synthesis.
Recycling vesicle → plasma membrane (5)
"At neutral pH the ligand-binding arm is free to bind another LDL particle": each receptor makes many trips.
Clinical / real-world · familial hypercholesterolaemia and statins

In familial hypercholesterolaemia, LDL-receptor mutations break this cycle at different points: no receptor made, receptor stuck in the ER, receptor that can't bind LDL, or (classically) a receptor that binds LDL but can't enter coated pits because its tail no longer binds AP2. LDL stays in the blood, giving early atherosclerosis and heart attacks, sometimes in childhood. Statins lower cell cholesterol synthesis, so cells make more LDL receptors and clear more LDL. PCSK9 inhibitors stop receptors being diverted to the lysosome, so more of them recycle (step 5).

Memory hook · "Bind, Bud, Bath, Break, Back"

Bind in the pit → Bud the coated vesicle → Bath in acid (late endosome, pH 5) → Break down LDL in the lysosome → receptor goes Back to the surface.

R Recall — endocytosis
  • Pinocytosis — "cell drinking", vesicles formed at the plasma membrane
  • Constant surface area despite endocytosis because — membrane is added back by exocytosis
  • Endocytosis starts at — clathrin-coated pits; vesicle forms within ~1 minute
  • First sorting station — early endosome; return route via recycling endosome
  • Early → late endosome as it moves — towards the nucleus on microtubules; stops recycling
  • Late endosome + lysosome = endolysosome
  • Four lysosome inputs — endocytosis, phagocytosis, macropinocytosis, autophagy
  • Phagocytes — macrophages and neutrophils
  • LDL adaptor in coated pits — AP2
  • LDL released from receptor at — pH ~5 (late endosome)
  • LDL receptor fate — recycled to the surface
